name: Suloev Stretch from Half Guard
summary: The Suloev Stretch is a back-control submission that captures a tripoding opponent's ankle and extends the leg while the torso is contained, loading the hamstring rather than folding the calf.
description: The Suloev Stretch captures an ankle from rear control against a tripod. It stretches the extended leg; half guard alone does not establish the finish.
target_area: Hamstring and posterior hip; knee at risk if the leg is twisted
overview:
The attacker is attached behind an opponent who has raised the hips into a tripod, with torso control and access to one ankle. Half guard is not the demonstrated finishing configuration. Sterling and Gonzalez distinguish the straight-leg stretch from sideways knee torque; obtaining the back is a separate prerequisite.

Control the torso from behind before reaching below the hips. Work only when the opponent's raised hips expose an ankle without sacrificing your balance. Reach down with the opposite hand and secure the lower leg while maintaining rear torso control. Arrange the leg so it extends in its natural line rather than rotating sideways at the knee.

Use a cooperative entry and stop at the aligned capture. Never drop onto the stretch, bounce the leg, or roll sideways while the ankle is fixed.

Instructional sources: [Aljamain Sterling and James Gonzalez — UFC 228 submission breakdown](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iHhOQwl1src); [ADCC — competition rules](https://adcombat.com/adcc-rules-regulations/).

defender.name: Suloev Stretch Defender
defender.description: Suloev Stretch from Half Guard (defender): A hand reaching from your back toward the ankle is an early cue to protect the leg. Use hand fighting before the ankle and torso are controlled together.
defender.overview:
The attacker is attached behind an opponent who has raised the hips into a tripod, with torso control and access to one ankle. Half guard is not the demonstrated finishing configuration. Sterling and Gonzalez distinguish the straight-leg stretch from sideways knee torque; obtaining the back is a separate prerequisite.

A hand reaching from your back toward the ankle is an early cue to protect the leg. Use hand fighting before the ankle and torso are controlled together. Maintain a stable base and address the rear attachment before raising the hips with a leg available.

Keep the captured leg aligned instead of rolling sideways against the ankle grip. Stop before a forced hamstring stretch or knee rotation develops. Recover the base only after the attacker has opened the ankle and torso controls.

Use a cooperative entry and stop at the aligned capture. Never drop onto the stretch, bounce the leg, or roll sideways while the ankle is fixed.

The early escape denies the rear hand access to the ankle and reduces the exposed tripod while the leg is still free. If the ankle and torso are already captured together, tap and let both controls open before rebuilding your base.

Before an ankle is captured, rebuilding base brings the elbows beside the ribs and the knees back beneath the body. Keep that elbow-knee connection while checking the rear attacker's hands: rising into a tripod still exposes the ankle, so the base change alone does not remove the submission threat.
key_principles: Recognize ankle access: A hand reaching from your back toward the ankle is an early cue to protect the leg.
Deny the grip early: Use hand fighting before the ankle and torso are controlled together.
Avoid an exposed tripod: Maintain a stable base and address the rear attachment before raising the hips with a leg available.
Do not twist away: Keep the captured leg aligned instead of rolling sideways against the ankle grip.
Tap to the capture: Stop before a forced hamstring stretch or knee rotation develops.
Move after the release: Recover the base only after the attacker has opened the ankle and torso controls.
